paras: The lynching of Archibald Pelon took place at Grayling, Michigan, in the early hours of November 7, 1888, when masked men took him from the sheriff and hanged him from a beam between two trees. Pelon had been arrested for allegedly assaulting two women near Beaver Creek, and no arrests for his killing were reported. The fullest wire dispatch noted that Michigan had seen no lynching in fifteen years.

According to the Crawford Avalanche, Grayling's local paper, on the afternoon of Monday, November 5, a man entered the home of Mrs. J. S. Crego of Beaver Creek, a woman of 63, and assaulted her. The same man was then said to have stopped at Arthur Marvin's house, asking the way to a lumber camp, and to have assaulted and choked Mrs. Marvin. Wire versions described the women as an old lady of 60 or "an aged widow" and a young married woman of 18, and the Rock Island Argus added that her husband was out hunting the attacker at the time.

T. E. Hastings of Beaver Creek tracked the suspect to the depot at Roscommon and seized him. Brought to Grayling on Tuesday morning, he was shackled and kept in the court house because the jail had no cells, and the Avalanche wrote that hundreds came to view him "as they would a wild beast." The paper reported that he had confessed and that Mrs. Marvin had identified him.

With "rumors of rescue and revenge" in town that afternoon, Sheriff McCullough moved the prisoner to a private residence and guarded him there himself. At about one o'clock in the morning, by the local account, a large body of masked and disguised men surrounded the house, overpowered the sheriff, and dragged Pelon down from an upper room. They took him to a small grove in the north part of the village, about thirty rods from the jail, where a scantling had been laid across two trees, and hanged him.
Once the sheriff was freed, a search party found the body still hanging, in handcuffs and leg shackles, at about 3 a.m. according to one version.

The body was turned over to Coroner Woodworth, who buried it; no report of an inquest verdict appears in the coverage. The Avalanche said the disguises were so good that no one was recognized and that none of the lynchers would probably be found. The Rock Island version claimed instead that the lynchers were known, though it, too, expected no legal action.

The Avalanche ran the story under "A Damnable Outrage! Judge Lynch Pronounces the Penalty of Death," calling the accused "a beast in human form," but it closed by regretting that "the majesty of the law should be trampled on in our midst." It named him as "Archibald Pelom, a Frenchman," with a "thoroughly bad" reputation, and no paper gave his race.

A short wire dated November 7 reached the New-York Tribune and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on November 8, the latter under the headline "A Fleud [Fiend] Lynched." A fuller dispatch, in the Camden Evening Telegram, was headlined "A Brute Who Assaulted Two Women is Strung to a Tree," and the Paw Paw True Northerner later ran the same account as "Judge Lynch Hangs a Brute." Kentucky papers reprinted the short wire the next day, the Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal adding that he had been "very properly hanged."

Weekly digests in Minnesota and Mississippi carried one-line notices in mid-November, while Michigan state-news columns named "Mrs. Frank Marvin, of Battle Creek" and a mob of twenty-five. At year's end the case appeared in published lists of the year's lynchings.

Reports differed on the size of the mob, given as fifty in the main wire, thirty in the Rock Island version and twenty-five in the Michigan state-news brief, while the local paper said only "a large body." The hour ranged from about 9 o'clock in the state-news brief to midnight in the wire and about one o'clock in the local account, which is the most detailed. Brief wires said he was taken "from the jail," but the local paper and the fuller dispatch place him in a private house under the sheriff's guard.

reader.title: Lynching of Archibald Pelon
bases: Masked men overpowered the sheriff, took a prisoner accused of assaulting two women from custody and hanged him from a beam between two trees (A1, A3, A10).

Pelon was hanged by a body of masked men, given as twenty-five to fifty, who took him by force from the sheriff, as punishment for alleged assaults on two women (A1, A3, A4, A11); the local paper said the law was 'trampled on' (A1).

The local Crawford Avalanche (A1) and independent wire and Michigan state-news versions (A3, A4, A5, A11) agree that masked men took Pelon from the sheriff at Grayling and hanged him, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Wire report (Grayling, Nov. 8)
accounts.gist: Sheriff hid him in a village house because the jail was unsafe; about midnight Tuesday fifty masked men hanged him in a grove thirty rods from the jail.

accounts.label: Variant wire (Rock Island)
accounts.gist: Thirty masked men took 'a dissolute character' from the sheriff early in the morning; the lynchers are known but unlikely to be prosecuted.

accounts.label: Brief wire (Nov. 7)
accounts.gist: Pelon, in jail for assaulting a girl or an old lady, was taken from the jail by masked men and hanged last night.

accounts.label: Michigan state-news brief
accounts.gist: Archie Pelan, charged with assaulting Mrs. Frank Marvin of Battle Creek, taken from the sheriff about 9 o'clock by twenty-five masked men and hung within the village.

info: Hanged about 1 a.m. on the night of Tuesday to Wednesday, after his capture Monday and arrival in Grayling Tuesday morning (local paper); wires put it about midnight Tuesday or 'last night' under a Nov. 7 dateline; digests say the 7th; one year list says Nov. 6.
A little grove in the north part of the village of Grayling, thirty rods from the jail; the assaults took place at Beaver Creek, and he was caught in the depot at Roscommon.
Archibald Pelon (also Arch Pelon, Archibald Pelom, Arch Peton, Archie Pelan); described by the local paper as 'a Frenchman' with a bad reputation. No paper gives his race.

Accused of assaulting Mrs. J. S. Crego of Beaver Creek, 63, at her home on Monday afternoon, and then Mrs. Marvin at Arthur Marvin's house; he was said to have confessed and to have been identified by Mrs. Marvin. Wires describe an old lady of 60 or aged widow and a young married woman (18); the Michigan state-news brief names Mrs. Frank Marvin of Battle Creek; some wires say 'a girl'.
Masked and disguised men; the local paper says no one was recognized, while the Rock Island version says the lynchers are known.

sources.note: Local account, fullest: assaults on Mrs. J. S. Crego of Beaver Creek and Mrs. Marvin; capture at Roscommon; sheriff overpowered at a private residence about 1 a.m.; grove in north of village; Coroner Woodworth; 'Archibald Pelom, a Frenchman'; no lynchers recognized.
quotes: the sheriff quietly removed him to a private residence where he remained personally on guard till about one o'clock in the morning
While little, if any sympathy is expressed for him, yet all must regret that the majesty of the law should be trampled on in our midst
The criminal's name was Archibald Pelom, a Frenchman, whose reputation was thoroughly bad.
